title: Finding Your Way Around the Keys
description: Learn the pattern of black and white keys so you can find any note, then try your first sharp and your first octave.

steps.title: How the keyboard repeats
steps.description: Look at the black keys. They come in little groups: two, then three, then two, then three, all the way up. That pattern is your map. C always sits just to the left of a group of two black keys. Find C, and you can count your way to any other note.

steps.title: Find middle C
steps.description: Middle C (C4) is the C nearest the middle of the keyboard. Find a group of two black keys near the center and press the white key just to its left.
steps.hint: It's the white key touching the left side of the two black keys. If the wrong C lights up, try the one next to it.

steps.title: Now D
steps.description: D is the white key tucked between those two black keys. Press D4, the one just above middle C.
steps.hint: From middle C, move one white key to the right.

steps.title: And E
steps.description: E is the white key just to the right of the two black keys. Press E4. C, D and E all live around that same pair of black keys.
steps.hint: Count up from middle C: C, D, E. Three white keys in a row.

steps.title: Your first black key
steps.description: Black keys are sharps and flats. The black key right after C is C# (C sharp), half a step higher. Press C#4, the left one of the two black keys just above middle C.
steps.hint: It's the black key just up and to the right of middle C.

steps.title: Two Cs at once
steps.description: An octave is the jump from one note to the next note with the same name. Play middle C and the C above it (C5) together. Notice how they blend, almost like a single note.
steps.hint: Count eight white keys up from middle C, counting middle C as one. Using both hands makes this easier.

steps.title: Where's C?
steps.description: Quick check before you move on. How do you spot a C on the keyboard?
